Chapter 5: The Impact of War on Family, Animals, and the City.
The longer the war dragged on, the more everyone connected to the zoo felt its weight. Warsaw, once buzzing with energy and color, changed into a city clouded by fear and uncertainty. You could hear soldiers’ boots on the streets, see checkpoints at every corner, and the sounds of gunfire and explosions—they became the background noise of daily life. Even the Żabińskis’ villa, which had always felt like a safe haven, couldn’t escape the pressure of occupation.
Imagine being a child in the middle of all this. Ryszard, the Żabińskis’ son, had to grow up fast. He learned when to keep quiet, how to spot danger, and somehow, he still found little sparks of joy when everything seemed dark.
And it wasn’t just the people feeling the strain. The animals at the zoo changed too. Some grew nervous, others became aggressive, but a few seemed to understand—they offered quiet companionship, almost as if they sensed how much it was needed. Antonina poured her heart into caring for them, even when food and supplies were scarce. Every time she fed or cleaned, it wasn’t just routine—it was an act of quiet rebellion, a way of saying, “Life goes on, no matter what.”
Inside the villa, the guests hiding there were transformed by the experience. Some discovered courage they didn’t know they had, while others battled fear and despair. Antonina and Jan did everything they could—offering comfort, encouragement, and a shoulder to lean on when hope seemed far away. The connections built in that house weren’t just friendships—they were lifelines, forged in the middle of danger and hope.
Meanwhile, outside the safety of the zoo, the city was changing in heartbreaking ways. The ghetto, once a lively part of Warsaw, became a place of suffering and loss. The Żabińskis saw it firsthand, and their determination to help only grew stronger. Jan’s work with the resistance became riskier, and Antonina’s role as a caretaker and confidante turned even more important. Word spread about the villa—a place where you might find safety, a little comfort, and a sense of humanity in a world turned upside down.
Through everything, the Żabińskis held onto the values that mattered most: compassion, courage, and a sense of responsibility to others. Even when the risks were overwhelming, they followed their hearts. The lessons they’d learned in the zoo—how fragile life can be, why empathy matters, and the incredible power of small acts of kindness—became the foundation for everything they did.
As the war stretched on, lines blurred—between human and animal, family and guest, home and refuge. The villa became a symbol of hope in a city shadowed by fear. It reminded everyone that even in the darkest moments, the urge to protect and care for others doesn’t disappear. The Żabińskis’ story isn’t just about surviving—it’s about the quiet heroism that shows up when ordinary people decide to do what’s right, no matter the cost.
